column4: The section places Adam in a garden before the fall; this neighboring promise names freedom from hunger, nakedness, and thirst, completing the protected setting that 20:119 adds to.
The section links its source root ض ح و to a road appearing in daylight; Adam is promised he will not be exposed to its heat (تَضْحَىٰ), making dawn a form of protection.
After Adam's lapse, his Lord chooses him, accepts his repentance, and guides him; this directly joins a fall to the return and guidance the section pairs.
The section's lost path is answered by Adam's promise: whoever follows God's guidance will not go astray or be wretched, specifying what guidance secures.
Moses describes his earlier self as among the ضَّالِّين; the section explicitly links ض ل ل to one who does not know which way to turn, so his words carry the lost-way sense.
Fleeing toward Midian, Moses asks his Lord to guide him to the sound way (يَهْدِيَنِي سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ); the path in the section is here an urgent request.
Moses finds (وَوَجَدَ) two women holding back their flock while others water theirs; the verse joins the section's finding verb to its meeting of path and herd.
After watering the women's flock, Moses withdraws to shade and says he needs whatever good his Lord sends; the scene makes shelter and provision meet in one prayer.
The daughter walks modestly to invite Moses to her father; this is the welcome at home that follows his help at the well in 28:24.
The father is told to hire Moses because he is strong and trustworthy; the verse turns shelter into a dependable place and livelihood.
The father offers Moses marriage to one of his daughters after his service; this is the household and marriage the section names in its life sequence.
The marriage offer is fixed to an eight- or ten-year term, with no injustice in the agreement; it makes the section's deferred time concrete inside Moses's new household.
After the term, Moses travels with his family and sees a fire, hoping for news or a burning brand; it is the section's distant fire that may offer direction and warmth.
The next verse calls Moses from the side of the valley at the fire; it supplies the voice and divine direction that the preceding fire-seeking scene has not yet revealed.
Moses sees a fire while traveling with his family and hopes to bring back news or a brand; this is the section's fire as a possible guide.
As Moses approaches the fire, he is called by name; this neighboring call resolves the search for guidance begun in 20:10.
Moses tells his family to wait as he sees fire and hopes to bring news or a burning brand; the same distant light is treated as a practical guide.
At the fire Moses is called and the presence is blessed; this next step supplies a speaker for the light he had approached in 27:7.
God recalls that He had already favored Moses once before (مَرَّةً أُخْرَىٰ); the section reads Moses's later provision as part of a remembered history of gifts.
The account turns to what was revealed to Moses's mother; this begins the infant's hidden passage from danger toward shelter described in the section.
The child is placed in a chest and cast into the river, yet God says He put love on Moses and that he would be raised under His eye; danger becomes guarded nurture.
Moses's sister offers someone to care for him, and he is returned to his mother for her eye to be cooled; this completes the shelter-and-reunion sequence.
God says He chose Moses for Himself; this follows the rescued childhood and makes the later guidance part of a sustained favor.
Pharaoh claims, 'Did we not raise you among us as a child?'; the section explicitly hears رب as owner and nurturer, while this is Pharaoh's human claim to have raised Moses.
Moses's mother is told to nurse him, cast him into the river if afraid, and not fear because he will be returned; this joins vulnerability, shelter, and promised guidance.
Pharaoh's household retrieves the child, though he is to become their enemy and grief; the section's sheltering image is shadowed by the danger of a protector's house.
Pharaoh's wife calls the child an eye's comfort, asks that he not be killed, and proposes adoption; this is a ruler's household sheltering an abandoned infant.
Moses's mother's heart empties and she nearly discloses him; this is a precise instance of the section's movement between concealment and telling.
Moses's sister watches him from a distance; her watching leads to the offer of a nursing household in 28:12.
The sister offers to direct Pharaoh's household to a family who will care for the infant; this is the specific household shelter the section describes.
Moses is returned to his mother so her eye may be cooled and she not grieve; this completes the protection promised in 28:7.
When Moses reaches maturity, God grants him judgment and knowledge; the verse supplies the growth from a cared-for child to an adult that the section's nurturing image implies.
Pharaoh divides the people, oppresses a group, and kills their sons; this is the human domination of the vulnerable that the section sets against the command not to crush an orphan.
God promises to favor those oppressed in the land and make them leaders and inheritors; the reversal answers Pharaoh's domination with protection and elevation.
A wall is repaired to protect the treasure of two orphan boys until maturity because their father was righteous; this makes hidden provision and a guardian's care literal.
A water drawer discovers Joseph in a well and calls him good news, a boy; this repeats the section's found-and-rescued child image in another Qur'anic story.
Joseph's buyer tells his wife to give the boy an honorable home, perhaps adopting him; the household's welcome closely echoes Moses being taken in.
Moses is sent to bring his people from darkness into light and remind them of God's days; this joins the section's path and light images within Moses's own story.
Moses tells his people that gratitude for God's favor brings increase; the verse gives a direct response to the section's command to speak of the Lord's blessing.
Moses reminds Israel that God appointed prophets, made them rulers, and gave what was not given others; this is a specific act of recounting past blessing.
Believers are reminded that they were few, afraid, sheltered, strengthened, and provided good things so they might be grateful; past protection becomes an ethical memory.
Qarun is told to seek the Hereafter with what God gave him and to do good as God did good to him; this states the return from received blessing to care for others.
The section links its source word عَائِل to need and future relief; this verse says fear of عَيْلَة (poverty) is answered by God's future enrichment.
The verse says God is the One who enriches (أَغْنَىٰ); it names the same specific change from need to sufficiency that the section recalls in 93:8.
This verse joins completion of a blessing to guidance on a straight path; it is the section's explicit meeting of sufficiency and being led.
God guides seekers of His pleasure through paths of peace, brings them from darkness into light, and guides them to a straight path; light and direction meet in one claim.
Revelation is made a light by which God guides, and the verse ends with guidance to a straight path; it brings the section's light and road into a single image.
People are said to prefer the nearer life; this is the choice opposite the section's claim that what comes after is better.
The Hereafter is called better and more enduring than the worldly life, giving the section's after/first contrast its direct Qur'anic formulation.
The speakers ask to have fighting deferred to a near term, then are told worldly enjoyment is little and the Hereafter better; this joins postponement to the value of what comes after.
The one who wants the immediate life receives only what God wills of it and then faces an appointed end; this sets a boundary around the section's promised future giving.
The one who seeks the Hereafter and strives for it is promised appreciated effort; this develops the section's contrast between the first and what follows.
What people are given is only the adornment of worldly life, while what is with God is better and lasting; this gives a concrete form to what passes and remains.
What people possess comes to an end, while what is with God remains; the verse states the passing-and-enduring relation behind the section's time meeting.
The Prophet is told not to strain his eyes toward worldly splendor, since his Lord's provision is better and more lasting; it joins provision with the section's future-facing measure.
For one mindful of God, He makes a way out; the neighboring promise in 65:3 adds unexpected provision, joining the section's road and sufficiency.
God provides from where a person does not expect and is sufficient for whoever trusts Him; this completes 65:2's way out with provision.
Guardians are commanded to give orphans their property and not consume or exchange it wrongly; this specifies how a caretaker must not take from the vulnerable.
Guardians must test orphans until maturity and then hand over their property, with limits on a poor guardian's use; the verse makes care temporary and accountable.
Those who consume orphan property unjustly are said to consume fire; this gives a severe boundary to the section's ban on crushing the orphan.
The command forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best manner until maturity; it makes the section's protection a concrete limit on power.
The orphan's property may be approached only in the best way until maturity; the following command to fulfill covenants makes protection a kept trust.
The verse commands justice toward orphan girls and other vulnerable children; it extends the section's orphan-care rule to a specific household vulnerability.
God is called الْقَاهِرُ فوق عباده, the subduer over His servants; the section names قهر as power-taking and contrasts God's sovereignty with a human's forbidden domination of an orphan.
The verse says there is no compulsion in religion and distinguishes guidance from error; it marks a boundary between being guided and forcing another.
Property may pass between people only through trade by mutual consent; this gives an explicit consent boundary to the section's warning against taking by force.
The pledge is made by believers' hands beneath God's hand; as a willing covenant, it contrasts the section's coercive hand that takes without consent.
The section identifies تَنْهَرْ as the Qur'anic verb for rebuking; here it is forbidden toward parents and replaced by noble speech, the exact sound contrast.
The next verse asks for mercy for parents as they raised the speaker young (رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا); it supplies the nurturing memory behind 17:23's gentle speech.
Moses and Aaron are told to speak gently to Pharaoh; even in a difficult encounter, the Qur'an makes softness of voice the chosen way.
The Prophet's gentleness is attributed to God's mercy, and harshness is said to drive people away; this shows what a soft response preserves against rebuke.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury; this directly contrasts the section's giving with harm in speech.
The verse warns that reminders and injury can nullify charity; it places a boundary on speaking about a gift that fits the section's command to tell blessing.
The verse orders giving the needy and traveler their due; it names the same vulnerable recipient class whose asking the section says not to rebuke.
If the speaker must turn away while awaiting mercy, the command is to use gentle words; this gives the exact response when a request cannot be met.
Righteousness includes giving wealth to orphans, needy people, travelers, and those who ask, as well as freeing captives; the verse gathers the section's vulnerable recipients.
The verse assigns a right in wealth to the asker and the deprived; it makes the needy person's claim part of provision, not an intrusion.
The next ayah says the believers' wealth contains a known right; this establishes the share whose recipients are named in 70:25.
The right belongs to the asker and the deprived; this completes 70:24 and makes the section's petitioner a recognized recipient.
The poor are described as restrained and not importuning people, though an uninformed observer may think them self-sufficient; this adds hidden need to the section's visible asker.
The righteous give food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving it; this makes care an actual transfer to the vulnerable.
They explain that they feed only for God's countenance and want neither repayment nor thanks; this states the motive behind 76:8's giving.
The denier of judgment is identified as one who repels the orphan; this is the direct opposite of the section's command not to crush him.
The same person does not urge feeding the poor; this adds a failure of mutual care beside the rebuff in 107:2.
The passage rebukes people for failing to honor the orphan; it names the opposite conduct to the section's command.
The next verse reproaches them for not urging one another to feed the poor; it completes the orphan-and-need pairing with shared responsibility.
They are accused of consuming inheritance greedily; this is a concrete form of taking from those whose property should be protected.
This verse itself says people love wealth fiercely; beside 89:19's charge of devouring inheritance, that desire is the appetite opposed to the section's provision and restraint.
The surah calls a moral act the steep path; the following verses define it through freeing and feeding, meeting the section's path image with its care commands.
The first deed on that steep path is freeing a neck; this adds release from domination to the section's prohibition on crushing.
The path next requires feeding on a day of hunger; this connects guided conduct to material need.
The one fed is an orphan close in relation; this makes the section's orphan care part of the steep path.
The path's next recipient is a needy person in misery; it adds the section's asker and poverty to the same moral sequence.
Believers ask for spouses and children as قُرَّةَ أَعْيُنٍ, comfort to their eyes; the phrase echoes the section's child returned so his mother's eye may be cooled.
A reward hidden from people is called قُرَّةِ أَعْيُنٍ; this joins the section's hidden blessing and eye-comfort language.
Night and day are made signs, with the night darkened and the day made visible for seeking provision; this ties concealment, light, and sufficiency.
The section names the root ل ي ل in its night image; this oath describes night as it covers, matching the covering half of the section's light-and-concealment meeting.
The paired oath names daytime as it appears (النَّهَارِ إِذَا تَجَلَّىٰ); it matches the section's daylight road becoming manifest.
This oath names the day as it displays the sun; it repeats the section's visible-light side in a distinct formulation.
The paired oath names night as it covers; this repeats the concealment side of the section's night-and-light meeting.
Night is made a garment and sleep a rest, while day is made for rising; it gives covering and emergence distinct functions.
Night is called a covering; this states directly the concealment half of the section's light meeting.
Day is made for livelihood; the following verse links the covering night to provision in daylight.
The sign is that daylight is stripped from night, leaving people in darkness; it states the visible world as a boundary between light and concealment.
God takes people by night, knows what they do by day, then awakens them for a term; this joins night, sleep-like concealment, and return.
God takes souls at death and during sleep, retaining some and sending others back until a term; this connects the night's covering to the grave's return.
Giving openly is good, while giving secretly to the poor may be better; this sets a context-sensitive boundary on the section's command to make blessing known.
Public mention of evil is disliked except by one who has been wronged; this marks a boundary between harmful disclosure and the section's positive telling of blessing.
God is named the First and Last, the Manifest and Hidden; this brings the section's after/first and concealment/disclosure pairings into one statement.
Every blessing people have is from God, and in distress they call upon Him; this states the source of the favors the section tells its audience to recount.
A crow shows Cain how to conceal his brother's corpse in the earth; this is the Qur'an's concrete burial scene behind the section's covered-dead image.
The human is caused to die and buried; this is the section's covered body in the earth.
The next verse says the human will be raised when God wills; it completes burial with new creation.
People are described as dead, given life, made to die, then restored to life; this gives the section's movement from burial to new creation a direct formulation.
Human beings are made from earth, returned to it, and brought out again; the verse joins burial and emergence in one sequence.
A man and his ruined town ask how God will revive it after its death; the man is made to die and restored, a concrete sign of new creation.
The verse traces human formation through the womb and compares revival to barren earth stirred by rain; it makes new creation visible in body and land.
God brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living, then gives life to earth after its death; this states both reversals in the section's buried-life image.
The challenge asks who can give life to bones after they have decayed; it names the very corpse that seems beyond return.
The answer is that the One who produced life the first time will revive it; this completes the decayed-bone question with new creation.
This verse asks whether the earth was made a container (كِفَاتًا); 77:26 names its contents, the living and the dead, grounding the section's burial image.
This verse names the living and the dead as earth's contents; 77:25 calls the earth a container, making the section's covered-body image a shared human condition.
After the described stages of human creation, the verse says people will surely die; it names the death that the section's grave image covers.
The next verse says people will be raised on the Resurrection Day; it completes 23:15's death with return.
Human beings are said to grow from the earth like plants; this gives the section's new creation a specific image of emergence.
The next verse says people return to the earth and are brought forth again; it completes the planting image with burial and resurrection.
Human life is traced from dust and stages in the womb through childhood, maturity, and old age; this makes the section's nurturing from state to state a broader human pattern.
Human life moves from weakness to strength and back to weakness and age; this renders the section's claim that the Lord carries a person from state to state.
